posts.title: [BDP] Golden Age of Piracy
posts.text: Thank you for taking time to vote and give support. I used BrickLink Studio2.0. Several years ago there were several LEGO CAD tools competing each other, but today I believe Studio 2.0 is first choice for almost anyone interested in LEGO digital design. As for the process, how do I go about it, for the Fort Ruin I got this idea while I was on the beach swimming. An image came up and as soon as I got out I drew a rough image on a piece of paper, and later that day started to develop it. Naturally, once you get going other ideas come out popping. Some made their way into the final design, others were scratched out immediately and some were abandoned due the limited number of pieces or poor stability. posts.text: @Timewhatistime Here you can see the solution I used, which is actually very similar to what you suggested: My approach is slightly different: I used a 1:20 reduction with a worm gear and a 20t gear, followed by a gear coupling with a 12t gear. This allowed me to strictly respect standard LEGO stud grid center distances while keeping the two output shafts (for hours and minutes) perfectly coaxial and parallel.

posts.title: [MOC / Ideas] "Just a Toy?" – Engineering a Working Analog Clock with Concentric Rings
posts.text: @Davidz90 Wow, I would have loved to see your project a few years ago when I first started working on this idea! The magnet solution is brilliant. Unfortunately, I don't think any official LEGO magnets in the current catalog have the right size or shape to pull that off, but it's a clever way around the problem. posts.title: [MOC / Ideas] "Just a Toy?" – Engineering a Working Analog Clock with Concentric Rings
posts.text: @Timewhatistime Thanks a lot for your feedback and for such an interesting suggestion! Using a single ring for each hand was actually my starting point: if you check out my very first model on the Ideas portal (the one I labeled as "horrible" in the Creator Updates section), you'll see that was precisely my initial goal. However, I quickly ran into real-world mechanical limits: The 11x11 Technic Curved Gear Racks (Part #68468) require additional elements just to stay connected. To prevent the mechanisms from jamming and destroying the gear reduction system, both the inner and outer surfaces of each ring had to remain completely flush and coplanar with the supporting frame. That’s how the double-ring structure was born. Doubling up the elements gave me a solid, self-supporting, and smooth ring assembly. But that introduced a new challenge: how to attach the hour hand? The only viable solution was to widen the profile by 1 stud to create an attachment point—which ultimately led to the "Ghost Hand Dilemma." In the renders, those attachment parts appear transparent, but those exact pieces don't actually exist in clear/transparent LEGO elements. So I couldn't translate that exact look into a physical build. In my real-life prototype, I had to use black pieces instead (ironically the furthest thing from transparent!), but it successfully proved the concept and met all structural requirements. That said, if you happen to experiment with a build that overcomes these physical constraints better than my current solution, I’d love to try integrating it into the design—and full credit will definitely go to you!

posts.title: [MOC / Ideas] "Just a Toy?" – Engineering a Working Analog Clock with Concentric Rings
posts.text: Hi @Wert, Yes, my clock operates using a motor with precise angular position control. These LEGO motors feature an output shaft encoder that constantly tracks position within a closed-loop system. By applying the desired position increment every n seconds (a customisable setting), the motor only runs for fractions of a second at regular intervals. This results in absolute timekeeping precision (zero cumulative error) and zero maintenance—something that is virtually impossible to achieve with spring, weight, or pendulum driven clocks. One of the biggest engineering challenges was actually minimising friction and internal forces to protect the LEGO elements and the motor, as well as reducing system noise. The result is a smooth drive train, which I’m still fine-tuning for even better efficiency. Additionally, the system automatically handles daylight saving time shifts (summer/winter time transitions) and integrates custom LED lighting for an overnight display effect that I personally really enjoy. If you’d like to see the lighting setup, I’ve included a few photos on the LEGO Ideas project page (though keep in mind those feature earlier iterations of the build). The classic debate between Analog and Digital is timeless and universal—we see it everywhere, from music and photography to fine engineering. I personally love both worlds, as each carries its own unique advantages, philosophy, and charm. Thanks a lot for sharing your thoughts—if you have any more feedback or suggestions, they are always very welcome!
